newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso urges Congress to vote on reforms.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso urges Congress to vote on reforms.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso on Monday called on Congress to approve reforms considered vital to Brazil's economic stability but which have been stuck at various stages of the lawmaking process.

In an address to mark the opening of a new session of parliament, Cardoso recalled his government's successes in taming Brazil's once rampant inflation, maintaining growth and improving wealth distribution.

"I believe the time has come to deepen this cycle with positive decisions regarding reform of the state, starting with the proposed constitutional amendments for the civil service, social security and the tax system," Cardoso said.

The government is seeking to revive its reform program following the approval in January by the Chamber of Deputies of a controversial constitutional amendment allowing Cardoso to stand for re-election next year.

The re-election amendment is due to be put to a second lower house vote next week. If approved, it moves to the Senate, opening the way for the Chamber of Deputies to vote on a bill to cut jobs in the civil service.

An amendment to reform the bankrupt pensions system is in the Senate but needs to be rewritten after being stripped of its most important points by the Chamber of Deputies last year. And a tax reform bill is on hold in a lower house committee.

The reforms are widely considered vital to Brazil's attempts to improve the country's fiscal situation and guarantee the long-term success of its inflation-slashing policies. But the government has run into entrenched opposition within Congress, especially to its proposals to cut public sector perks and job guarantees.

Cardoso, who last week traveled to Britain and Italy to personally address institutional investors on his government's commitment to reform, reminded Congress that Brazil had seen economic growth for five consecutive years.
"We have in our hands the key to fundamental decisions to turn confidence into a certainty that (Brazil) has finally found its path," the president said.
